content: Asthma is the most prevalent chronic respiratory condition globally, affecting approximately 334 million individuals, including both adults and children. Despite the availability of effective treatments, such as inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), adherence to these maintenance medications remains suboptimal. Poor adherence to ICS is associated with increased asthma symptoms, more frequent exacerbations, higher rates of hospitalizations, and greater healthcare utilization. Critically, inadequate use of asthma medications is a significant contributor to asthma-related mortality. The potential impact of digital interventions on improving medication adherence and asthma-related outcomes remains uncertain. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of digital interventions in enhancing adherence to maintenance treatments for asthma. To achieve this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including clusterand quasi-randomized trials, were identified through comprehensive searches of the Cochrane Airways Trials Register, trial registries, and reference lists of primary studies. The most recent search was conducted on June 1, 2020, with an additional search in October 2021, although the latter was not fully incorporated into the analysis. Studies included participants of all ages with a clinical diagnosis of asthma who were receiving maintenance treatment. Digital adherence interventions were compared to non-digital interventions or usual care. A total of 40 parallel RCTs involving 15,207 participants were included in the review, with eight additional studies ongoing. The sample sizes of the included studies ranged from 18 to 8,517 participants, with a median of 339. The duration of the interventions varied from two to 104 weeks. Most studies (29 out of 40) reported adherence to maintenance medication as the primary outcome, while other commonly reported outcomes included asthma control and quality of life. The risk of selection bias was generally low or unclear, but there was a high risk of performance and detection biases due to the inability to blind participants, personnel, or outcome assessors. Additionally, 25% of the studies exhibited a high risk of attrition bias and selective outcome reporting. Meta-analyses were conducted to assess the effects of digital interventions on several outcomes, including adherence (16 studies), asthma control (16 studies), asthma exacerbations (6 studies), unscheduled healthcare utilization (4 studies), lung function (7 studies), and quality of life (10 studies). The pooled results indicated that digital interventions may improve adherence to maintenance medication, with a mean increase of 14.66 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI]: 7.74 to 21.57; low-certainty evidence). This improvement is likely to be clinically significant, particularly for individuals with poor baseline adherence. Subgroup analyses revealed that electronic monitoring devices (EMDs) were associated with a 23-percentage-point improvement in adherence compared to control (95% CI: 10.84 to 34.16; 7 studies), while short message services (SMS) were associated with a 12-percentage-point improvement (95% CI: 6.22 to 18.03; 4 studies). No significant differences were observed between interventions with an in-person component versus fully digital interventions, adherence feedback, single versus multiple digital components, or participant age. Digital interventions were also found to likely improve asthma control, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.31 (95% CI: 0.17 to 0.44; moderate-certainty evidence). Although this represents a small effect, it is likely to be clinically significant. There was low-certainty evidence suggesting that digital interventions may reduce asthma exacerbations, with a risk ratio of 0.53 (95% CI: 0.32 to 0.91). The impact of digital interventions on unscheduled healthcare utilization was less clear, with some studies reporting no effect or a worsening effect. Data on school or work absences were not included in the meta-analysis due to variability in reporting and the limited number of studies. Regarding lung function, digital interventions were associated with a slight improvement in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of 3.58% predicted (95% CI: 1.00% to 6.17%; moderate-certainty evidence). However, this change is unlikely to be clinically significant, as it falls below the 12% threshold typically considered meaningful. Digital interventions were also associated with a likely increase in quality of life (SMD: 0.26; 95% CI: 0.07 to 0.45; moderate-certainty evidence), although the effect size was small and may not be clinically significant. Participants generally expressed positive attitudes toward digital interventions, indicating their acceptability. However, no data were available on the cost-effectiveness or adverse events associated with these interventions. The overall confidence in the evidence was reduced due to risks of bias and inconsistency across studies. In conclusion, digital interventions may lead to a substantial improvement in adherence to asthma maintenance medications (low-certainty evidence). There is moderate-certainty evidence suggesting that these interventions likely improve asthma control to a clinically significant degree and enhance quality of life, although they have little or no effect on lung function. There is also low-certainty evidence that digital interventions may reduce asthma exacerbations. Subgroup analyses indicate that EMDs may improve adherence by 23%, while SMS interventions may improve adherence by 12%. Interventions incorporating in-person elements and adherence feedback may offer additional benefits for asthma control and adherence, respectively. Future research should prioritize the use of percentage adherence as a standard outcome measure to facilitate comparisons across studies and meta-analyses. Additionally, validated questionnaires should be employed to assess adherence and other relevant outcomes.
